This was my fourth LEGO game that I 100% completed. I REALLY don't like this one, not even because it's about the new trilogy, but because this game is actually a nothing burger. I'm not sure if TT was planning on making a separate LEGO game for each new Star Wars episode, but this game feels out of place considering that there isn't a "Last Jedi" or "Rise of Skywalker" game (not that I want those, no sir). We have The Skywalker Saga so there is really no point in playing this unless you either just want to or you want to "master" it.
With that being said, there were ONE cool thing about it. I thought the shooting battles were fun and it brought a dynamic not seen in LEGO games before. That's it...

I thought the whole game sucked though, the missions were not memorable at all, the characters were carbon copies of other assets, and you can't even 100% the game without buying the DLCs (that's a Steam problem though). It felt like you were better off being a character with a blaster than a Jedi or Sith, they felt flimsy and weak. Their superpower or "ult" was nothing, and the AI were dumb as bricks. The flying missions were okay I guess.
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, don't get me started on the voice acting and voice cues. Obviously they took some lines from the movie, but it felt like I was watching a 2010 LEGO stop-motion video, it was just so bad and made me want to go to bed instead of play video games. It took me so long to beat the game (I started around Christmas time last year and completed it in March) because I really just did not want to play the game at all.

I mean, that's pretty much it, the game sucks and it's probably one of the worst LEGO games out there, and there are some pretty bad ones.

cons:

I grew up playing LEGO games like Lego Star Wars, Lego Batman, and Lego Indiana Jones, and honestly, Lego Star Wars: The Force Awakens brought me right back to my childhood. The humor, the chaos, breaking everything for studs, replaying levels for collectibles, it felt like reconnecting with a part of myself I forgot I missed this much.

This game also helped me get through final exam season. Sounds dramatic maybe, but after stressful days full of assignments and exhaustion, opening this game at night genuinely made things feel lighter. It became my comfort game during one of the most tiring parts of my semester 😭

I bought the game during a sale and decided to go all in with the Season Pass plus the Phantom Limb Level Pack and Droid Character Pack (since those two aren’t included in the Season Pass). And honestly? Completely worth it. There are SO many characters, fun moments, and iconic scenes packed into this game that it constantly kept me smiling.

The gameplay itself was also surprisingly fresh. The new mechanics made the experience feel more modern while still keeping that classic LEGO charm I grew up with. It’s simple, fun, relaxing, and somehow still incredibly entertaining even after hours of playing.

Getting 100% achievements on this game honestly felt special to me. It wasn’t just completion for the sake of achievements, it felt like reliving a piece of my childhood during a stressful time in my life.

Now I really hope I can buy Lego Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga someday for an even bigger LEGO Star Wars experience 😭

[h1][b] Reseña de LEGO® STAR WARS™: The Force Awakens[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
LEGO® STAR WARS™: The Force Awakens es la versión “todo público” (pero con chistes que a veces pegan mejor que el guion) de una aventura de Acción/Aventura en tercera persona donde disparas, resuelves rompecabezas y rompes literalmente TODO… porque si no destruyes el escenario, ¿de verdad jugaste un LEGO?

La propuesta es clara: revivir la película con humor, coleccionables y caos controlado, alternando secciones de combate, plataformas y puzzles ligeros. La primera impresión es como abrir una caja de piezas: al inicio es emocionante, luego te das cuenta de que vas a armar el mismo halcón por quinta vez… pero ahora con otro sombrero.

Y sí: tiene cooperativo local/online, pantalla dividida y Remote Play Together, o sea que puedes arrastrar a un amigo a sufrir contigo desde el sillón… o desde la nube, como todo en 2026.

[h2]Lo Lado Luminoso y lo Lado “¿En serio, BB-8?”[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
  Humor LEGO constante: convierte momentos “serios” en comedia sin pedir permiso.  
  Cooperativo y pantalla dividida: ideal para jugar en familia o para discutir por quién se queda los studs.  
  Compatibilidad total con mando + Remote Play Together: cómodo y perfecto para jugar tirado como un Hutt.  
  69 logros de Steam: una lista larga para los que necesitan validación digital.  
  Steam Cloud: cambias de PC y tu obsesión coleccionista te sigue fielmente.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
  Dificultad bajita: más “aventura” que “desafío”; la Fuerza aquí es el piloto automático.  
  Fórmula LEGO muy conocida: si ya jugaste otros LEGO, esto es “más de lo mismo” con otra piel galáctica.  
  Rompecabezas poco exigentes: la mayoría se resuelven con la técnica ancestral de “pega hasta que funcione”.  
  Comunidad tranquila: 19 jugadores actuales… la Resistencia tiene más gente en una fila de café.  
  Depende del material base: si la historia de The Force Awakens no te compra, aquí tampoco hace milagros.

Unlike your typical Lego Star Wars games, which normally focus on a trilogy or a series of episodes, Lego Star Wars: The Force Awakens is based on a singular movie of the franchise: Episode VII. But despite the fact that The Lego Group and TT Games couldn't help but remind us that they're still making these things, no matter how unusual the decision to create a game centered around a single entry in the Star Wars universe, did it still turn out well?

Like the previous game, Lego Star Wars III: The Clone Wars (8/10), players start off in a fairly engaging prologue, this time focusing on the ending events of Episode VI, as they play through the destruction of the Death Star II's shield generator, the final duel against Emperor Palpatine, and the ultimate demise of the massive battle station. Entering the events of Episode VII, which takes place decades later, Luke Skywalker has now gone missing, hidden among the stars, with the Resistance attempting to locate his whereabouts while trying to keep some newly found information safe from the First Order, as brave pilot Poe Dameron hides the remaining map fraction inside of his droid companion, BB-8, who narrowly escapes on the desert planet of Jakku. (History seemingly repeats itself after Episode IV, huh?) As players are thrown into the adventure, they will be introduced to new mechanics that expand well upon the gameplay of the Lego Star Wars game series, such as multi-builds, which allow you to build a choice of several different models from the same pile of Lego bricks, droid computer outlets that now offer section-rotating puzzles, (though I'd rather the game not confirm their placement automatically as we turn them), handle bars that can be pulled by strong characters, and other mechanics that keep the adventure thrilling. You'll even come up to hallways and trenches in which you hide behind walls for cover while firing your blaster against enemies to progress forward, something fairly reminiscent of Sega's Star Wars Trilogy Arcade game (which was only somewhat nerve-racking to me as a kid. And no, I haven't done a proper review for it). Jedi characters can even use the Force in lieu of a blaster in these areas! It looks like someone in the developer team was indeed thinking! And new to the Lego Star Wars game series, the characters now use actual speech instead of mumbling, their dialogue being re-used from the original movies, and many new lines being recorded from the original voice actors! (Though, sometimes it does feel excessive.) A convenient alteration that addresses the tedious issue of searching for characters in the Clone Wars entry, you can now purchase unlocked characters straight from the character selection menu. Additionally, Power Brick settings are now saved, and they can easily be turned on and off, via the character wheel. Remember how the previous game's Minikits broke the tradition of collecting vehicle model sections by having you collect Minifigure parts instead? Well, now we're back to vehicles again! Specifically, Microfighters that you can fly around anywhere and take on certain challenges with. You do still collect bonus Minifigures, but they are frozen in Carbonite Bricks that have to be thawed in the Resistance Base on D'Qar. As for the ten, rather than six, different chapters you play through, they are now broken up into sub-chapters, allowing you to easily access a specific section if you missed any Minikits during your first session in Free Play. And the Steam achievements even have some fun references!

Though it does do a lot to expand upon the principles of what makes a Lego Star Wars game, there are actually many issues that I cannot easily ignore, especially the several irritating game-breaking bugs that it has, which I will get into in a moment. Throughout the game, there are several different hint projectors which you have to hit to get a tutorial from, but they really don't need to be used throughout the entire game, only the first level or so. A few environments, such as Palpatine's lair, have materials with roughness and normal maps that are mostly uniform and uninteresting. While the color palette of this game is mostly pleasing, there are some parts of it that look absolutely ugly. For example, at least one lightspeed tunnel in a cutscene is overly saturated. (The tunnels do often bear an inconsistent appearance, by the way.) Here's an important rule about color palettes: only use the most saturated colors on the things you want to draw attention to, such as the characters, so that they stand out from the environment. Anyway, the ugliest of the color palettes was on the Starkiller Base in free roam, which had some abhorrent, cyan lighting! In the rest of the galaxy, much of the lighting is what you would expect it to be, but at other times, it feels rather flat, especially in dense environments, like the forest on Takodana. And I'm thinking: come on! Where's the ambient occlusion? Where's the contrast? But what irritated me the most out of anything else in this game was the technical issues. Yes, the technical issues I brought up just at the top of this paragraph. And they haven't been addressed in YEARS! Character dialogue and sound becomes too quiet when your camera is not even that far from them. In Free Play, the Minikit detector is mostly accurate, but at fewer times, it is absolutely misleading. In The Eravana, there's a shooting section where BB-8 can easily get stuck in the ceiling. And once that happens, there's no way to get him out without restarting the level! To avoid this, make sure you're playing as Han or Chewie, with BB-8 in the Player 2 slot. Any character that isn't in one of the slots will get stuck, but they will rejoin you after you pass through the next door. In another major problem during Free Play in Starkiller Sabotage, I couldn't use thermal detonators to target and blow open a silver door. I even saw some barely visible, blue wireframe of developer geometry in front! There are a handful of several other game-breaking bugs that will force you to restart a level once or twice. But the absolute worst problem I experienced was with the vehicles! For whatever reason, during both cutscenes and gameplay, the vehicles happened to lag or stutter, while everything else ran smoothly. Depending on... I don't know what was going on, but sometimes the vehicles will only stutter, or they'll freeze for WAY TOO MANY SECONDS TOO LONG! This was especially a problem in the Starkiller Destruction bonus level, which I had no way of finishing, due to this absolute pain of an issue. Certain objects that use physics simulations also exhibit this problem. I did play this game once on the Xbox 360, years ago, with absolutely no issues, at least not that I can recall. So, maybe you'll have a better experience on certain consoles. As for the DLC, it practically added nothing new, but some bits and pieces of it were decently engaging, especially in the Escape From Starkiller Base level.

To sum it all up, Lego Star Wars: The Force Awakens does much to improve the series, and it does much to harm the series as well. Though this particular Lego gaming experience may have a few frustrating technical issues, it's only because of how the Force was with me that I didn't slash my computer with a lightsaber. Isn't that right, Kylo Ren?

Final Score: 7.75/10

This is a perfectly fine addition to the LEGO canon that doesn't wow as much as either Skywalker Saga or the original Complete Saga. It is a halfway house of sorts between the two, and it lacks both the complete nature of the latter and the dynamic hub of the former. You can tell in retrospect that the developers were building up to a greater and more fully realized world. Because this is only for material surround TFA, it lacks completeness, and some of the levels feel too minimal to matter in the scope of the plot. I did appreciate the bonus missions, both those included with the base and the DLCs, as they often gave an alternate perspective to events of the main storyline. The grind stage of this LEGO game feels a little more tedious than I would have thought, but I think it's because some of the hub worlds have weird map designs that don't allow for easy travel across them.

Quelqu'un pour qui ce serais le premier jeu LSW je peux comprendre son avis positif, par contre ayant comme point de repère LSW La Trilogie Originale je trouve que le jeu est bâclé.
Le tracking de la camera n'est pas réussi, on ne voit rien.
Tout le gameplay est lent, les constructions multiples et autres interactions ne sont pas intuitives.
L'ennui auquel je ne m'attendais pas lorsqu'on se retrouve entre deux niveaux dans une sorte de "hub" vide et trop grand.
On sent un manque de fluidité dans l'enchainement des énigmes, les QTE ne sont pas nécessaires et sont codés à la va-vite.
On perd le côté fun/libre/arcade pour une sorte d'immersion ratée et ennuyeuse, des décisions de direction artistique qui se concentrent sur le "hey t'as vu comme ils sont beaux mes graphismes de près!"
Bref pour moi ce jeu est une déception, je me suis arrêté à un niveau dans le Faucon Millenium où BB-8 est resté bloqué dans le plafond après une cinématique, sans être en mesure de le débloquer ou revenir au dernier checkpoint, je m'avoue vaincu, j'ai désinstallé le jeu.
Ma patience a des limites et ce jeu les a atteint rapidement, j'imagine que la suite du gameplay est toute aussi décevante, vraiment ça fait mal au coeur de voir ça puisque la licence a un potentiel énorme, on dirait que le jeu n'a pas été fait par des passionnés et n'a pas été testé.
Ah et les 2 minutes de chargement au début, sur des cinématiques qu'on ne peut pas passer, où l'on se demande si notre manette est toujours connectée à la console/pc sans aucune indication affichée lorsqu'on appuie sur une touche, c'est pas envisageable pour un jeu "moderne".
Pareil pour la lenteur du menu, la sélection des niveaux, ça donne l'impression que tout a été codée à la va-vite.
Ce jeu n'est pas défendable.
